uncited: Volume-Surface Hybridization is a rendering strategy that combines explicit surface geometry (meshes or isosurfaces) with implicit volumetric data to optimize computational cost and representation fidelity .
It solves the problem of efficiently rendering scenes containing both discrete surfaces and continuous volumetric fields by using surface intersections to limit or guide volume integration .

It sets itself apart from pure volume rendering by prioritizing surface geometry intersection to limit volume integration, and from pure mesh rendering by retaining the ability to render internal volumetric structures up to the surface boundary .
The family shares the core mechanism of using surface geometry to define integration bounds or sampling regions for volume data.
**Surface Detection:** For a given camera ray, the nearest intersection with a surface (mesh or isosurface) is determined.
**Integration Limiting:** Volume ray marching is restricted to the interval $[t_{min}, t_{max}]$, where $t_{min}$ is the near clipping plane and $t_{max}$ is the surface hit distance .
**Compositing:** The final color is a blend of the volume contribution (up to $t_{max}$) and the surface contribution (at $t_{max}$) .
The concept of hybrid rendering has evolved to address the limitations of pure volume or pure surface methods.
Early work focused on combining ray casting with rasterization to improve performance .
Modern implementations often use neural representations or advanced BVH structures to manage the complexity of hybrid scenes .
